title: Interrogate a Decision
blurb: Takes a decision you have already half-made and finds the assumptions you did not know you were making — then tells you what evidence would change your mind.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: The decision you are leaning toward, and why
input.placeholder: e.g. We should rebuild the onboarding flow in-house rather than buy, because…
input.seed: We should build our onboarding flow in-house rather than buying a vendor solution. Our needs are unusual, the vendors we looked at all assume a self-serve signup, and we think we can ship it in about six weeks with the two engineers currently between projects.

cells.title: Extract the case you actually made
cells.intent: Separates the argument from the conclusion. Most people cannot see their own reasoning until it is listed back to them.
cells.prompt:
Read the decision below. List only the claims the author actually made, one per line, in their own terms. Do not evaluate them. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.decision}}
demo: Our requirements are unusual enough that vendor products will not fit.
Every vendor evaluated assumes a self-serve signup motion.
Two engineers are currently available with no competing commitment.
The build is roughly a six-week effort.
Building is therefore cheaper or better than buying.

cells.title: Surface what was assumed, not argued
cells.intent: The load-bearing beliefs that were never stated out loud — because they felt too obvious to say.
cells.prompt:
Below are the explicit claims. Identify the unstated assumptions each one rests on — the beliefs that must be true for the claim to hold, but which were never argued. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{stated}}
demo: That "unusual requirements" are genuinely structural, rather than habits that hardened into requirements.
That the six-week estimate covers a first version, and that a first version is what ships — no ongoing maintenance is priced in anywhere.
That the two engineers stay available for the whole six weeks, which has not been true of any previous window.
That onboarding is a solved problem once built, rather than a surface that changes every time the product does.
That the cost of being wrong is symmetric — that an in-house build is as reversible as a vendor contract. It is not.

cells.title: Build the strongest case against
cells.intent: Not a list of risks. The actual argument a smart person who disagrees with you would make.
cells.demo:
The six weeks is not the cost. The cost is the next four years, during which onboarding is the surface most exposed to every product change you make, and the two engineers who built it have moved on. A vendor amortises that maintenance across every customer; you would be amortising it across one.

The "unusual requirements" claim is also doing more work than it can bear. Every team believes this, and it is true perhaps a fifth of the time. The evaluation found that vendors assume self-serve signup — but that is one requirement, not an architecture, and it is the kind of thing a vendor will meet if you are a large enough account or willing to sit slightly off the happy path.

And the availability of two engineers is not an argument for building. It is an argument that you have two engineers. Those are different, and conflating them is how organisations end up owning software they never chose to own.

cells.title: What would change your mind
cells.intent: Turns each assumption into something checkable this week. This is the cell that makes the notebook actionable rather than merely clever.
cells.prompt:
For each assumption, state what observation would disprove it and the cheapest way to check within one week. Return a table with columns: Assumption, Would be disproved by, Check this week. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{assumptions}}

rows: A vendor demo that handles 80% of them out of the box
Send your top 10 requirements to two vendors and ask them to mark each yes/no/partial
Six weeks is the real cost
Any comparable internal build that shipped and stayed shipped at estimate
Pull the last three internal tools you built. Compare estimate to actual, and check who maintains them now
Either one being pulled onto something else in the last two quarters
Ask their manager for a written commitment through the window. The answer itself is the data
Your onboarding changing more than twice a year
Count the onboarding-related tickets from the last 12 months
No credible path back to a vendor after 6 months in
Ask what the migration off your own build would cost. If nobody can answer, it is not reversible

cells.title: Where this leaves you
cells.intent: A position, not a summary. The notebook should end by being useful.
cells.demo:
The decision is not wrong, but it is currently being made on the wrong evidence. Three of the five load-bearing assumptions can be tested for roughly a day of effort each, and two of them — maintenance cost and engineer availability — have historical data sitting in systems you already own.

Run the vendor requirement-marking exercise and pull the estimate-versus-actual on your last three internal builds. If vendors clear 80% and your internal builds ran at 2x, buy. If vendors clear under half and your builds land near estimate, build with confidence you do not currently have.

The thing not to do is decide this week on the grounds that two engineers happen to be free.

title: Meeting Notes → Commitments
blurb: Separates what was actually decided from what was merely discussed, then finds every commitment nobody owns. The orphans are the point.
teaches: Extract — pull structure out of mess

input.label: Raw meeting notes — messy is fine
input.placeholder: Paste whatever you actually typed during the meeting.
input.seed:
Q3 planning sync — Tues
- Priya walked through the churn numbers, worse in SMB than we thought
- long discussion about whether pricing is the cause. Dan thinks packaging, Priya thinks onboarding
- agreed we're not changing price this quarter
- someone should pull the cohort data by plan tier before we decide anything
- Marco mentioned the enterprise renewal list needs a pass, said he'd look
- maybe worth talking to 5-10 churned accounts? felt like everyone nodded
- Dan to draft the packaging alternatives, before the exec review
- we didn't get to the roadmap item, pushed to next week
- Priya raised that support ticket volume is up 30%, no one picked it up

cells.title: Decisions vs. discussion
cells.intent: Meetings blur these constantly. A thing said with confidence is not a thing decided.
cells.prompt:
Classify each substantive item in these notes as Decided, Discussed only, or Deferred. Include the evidence phrase. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.notes}}

rows: "agreed we're not changing price this quarter"
Cause of SMB churn — packaging vs onboarding
"felt like everyone nodded" — this is not agreement

cells.title: Commitments, with owners
cells.intent: Every action, who holds it, and how confident that ownership actually is.

rows: Soft — "said he'd look" is not a commitment
Pull cohort data by plan tier

cells.title: The orphans
cells.intent: The three or four things everyone assumes are handled and nobody is holding. This is where meetings actually fail.
cells.prompt:
List the commitments with no firm owner or no date, and for each say what will happen if nothing changes. Be blunt. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{commitments}}
demo: **Cohort data by plan tier** — no owner. This is a prerequisite for the packaging-vs-onboarding decision, which means that decision is currently blocked on nobody.
**Churned account interviews** — no owner. Group nods are the single most reliable predictor of a task that never happens.
**Support volume up 30%** — no owner, and it was raised in a churn conversation. Nobody connected it to the churn discussion happening in the same room.
**Enterprise renewal pass** — Marco, softly. "Said he'd look" survives about nine days without a date attached.

cells.title: The message that fixes it
cells.intent: A follow-up that names the orphans without blaming anyone. Ready to send.
cells.demo:
**Q3 planning — what we settled and what we did not**

Decided: no price change this quarter.

Still open: whether SMB churn is a packaging or an onboarding problem. Dan and Priya have opposing reads and we did not resolve it.

Carrying:
- **Dan** — packaging alternatives, before exec review
- **Marco** — enterprise renewal pass. Can you put a date on it?

Four things came up that nobody picked up, and one of them is blocking the churn decision:

1. **Cohort data by plan tier.** We cannot settle packaging-vs-onboarding without it. Who owns this?
2. **Churned account interviews, 5–10.** There was general agreement but no name attached.
3. **Support ticket volume, up 30%.** Raised at the end and not discussed — worth noting we were talking about churn at the time.
4. Roadmap item, moved to next week.

If I have mischaracterised anything, correct me and I will re-send.

title: Find the Hole in This Plan
blurb: Reads a plan for its dependency structure rather than its content, then names the failure that is both most likely and least watched.
teaches: Plan — sequence, dependency, failure

input.label: The plan, in whatever shape it exists
input.placeholder: Bullet points are fine. Prose is fine.
input.seed:
Launch the new billing system by end of Q4.
- Nov: finish the migration script, dual-write to old and new
- Nov 15: finance signs off on the reconciliation report
- Dec 1: cut over 10% of accounts, monitor for a week
- Dec 8: cut over the rest
- Dec 15: decommission the old system
- Sarah leads, one backend engineer, finance reviews weekly
- Comms to customers go out Dec 1

cells.title: The dependency chain nobody drew
cells.intent: Plans are written as timelines and executed as dependency graphs. This makes the graph visible.
cells.prompt:
Extract the real dependency chain from this plan — what must be true before each step can begin. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.plan}}
demo: Migration script complete → dual-write can begin → reconciliation data exists
Reconciliation data exists → finance can review → finance sign-off (Nov 15)
Finance sign-off → 10% cutover (Dec 1)
10% cutover + one clean week → full cutover (Dec 8)
Full cutover + stability → decommission (Dec 15)
Customer comms (Dec 1) → runs in parallel, gated on nothing, reversible by nothing

cells.title: Single points of failure
cells.intent: Where the chain has no redundancy — in people, in time, and in the ability to undo.

rows: No second person can debug the migration script. Illness or attrition stops the chain entirely.
Every downstream date is hard-wired to it. A one-week slip lands the full cutover on Dec 15 — decommission day.
Seven days between full cutover and decommissioning the only fallback. Billing problems surface on a monthly cycle, not a weekly one.
Sent at 10% cutover. Once sent, the timeline is public and slipping becomes an external event, not an internal one.
Dec 15–31 has the thinnest staffing of the year and the plan puts decommissioning at its edge.

cells.title: Most likely, least watched
cells.intent: Risk registers list everything. This names the one that will actually happen.
cells.prompt:
Of these failure points, identify the one that is simultaneously most probable and least attended to in the plan. Explain why it is invisible. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{spof}}
cells.demo:
The seven days between full cutover and decommissioning.

It is the most likely to hurt because billing is a monthly-cycle system, and a week of monitoring cannot surface a class of bug that only appears at month-end close, on proration, on annual renewals, or on any account whose cycle falls outside that window. You will have decommissioned your only fallback before the first full billing cycle completes on the new system.

And it is invisible because it does not look like a risk. It looks like a schedule. Every other item in this plan has a person or a review attached; this one is just two dates sitting next to each other, and the gap between them was almost certainly set by the quarter boundary rather than by anything about billing.

The finance sign-off date gets attention because it has a name on it. This one has nobody, which is exactly why it will be the one.

cells.title: Cheapest insurance
cells.intent: What to change, ordered by cost. Not "add buffer" — specific moves.
demo: **Move decommission to after one full billing cycle closes on the new system.** Costs nothing but a date change, and removes the highest-probability failure in the plan outright.
**Delay customer comms to Dec 8.** Nothing customer-visible happens at 10% cutover. Sending on Dec 1 buys no benefit and converts every subsequent slip into a public one.
**Have a second engineer read the migration script.** Half a day. Turns the single person-dependency into a two-person one for the part that matters.
**Put a named date on what "monitor for a week" means passing.** Right now the Dec 8 gate is a vibe. Define the three numbers that must hold.
**Ask finance for a provisional sign-off on the report format now**, so Nov 15 is a data review and not a format argument. This is where sign-offs actually slip.

title: One Idea, Five Audiences
blurb: Renders the same concept for five different readers, then shows you which version you could not write — because that is where your own understanding is thin.
teaches: Translate — same idea, different reader

input.label: The thing you need to explain
input.placeholder: A technical concept, a strategy, a decision.
input.seed:
We are moving from a monolith to event-driven services, starting with the billing domain.
constraint: Be specific enough that two colleagues would disagree about the next step — that disagreement is the point of this notebook (The thing you need to explain).

cells.title: The load-bearing idea
cells.intent: Strip it to the one sentence everything else is decoration on.
cells.demo: Parts of the system that currently have to agree with each other in real time will instead tell each other what happened and carry on — starting with billing, because that is where the cost of waiting is highest.

cells.title: Five renderings
cells.intent: Same idea, five readers. Note the third column — what each version deliberately throws away.

rows: Billing is currently the slowest thing we do and the most expensive thing to change. We are separating it so it can move without the rest of the system holding it up. Six months, one team, no customer-visible change.
All mechanism. An exec who asks "how" will get nothing from this.
Instead of billing calling six services and waiting, it publishes an event and the others react. You will write handlers, not call chains. The hard part is that ordering is no longer guaranteed.
The reason. Tells them what to do, not why anyone chose it.

Yes, we are trading strong consistency for availability in one domain, and yes, that means eventual consistency bugs. We think billing is where that trade pays because reconciliation already exists there as a batch process. If it does not pay there, we stop.
Confidence. Deliberately — this reader distrusts certainty more than they distrust risk.
Nothing changes for you. Invoices, timing, and totals stay exactly as they are.
Everything. Which is correct — the honest version of this for a customer is that it is none of their business.
Right now one kid has to ask five others before doing anything, and everyone waits. We are letting them shout what they did and keep going.
Precision, entirely. But it is the version that reveals whether you understand it.

cells.title: Which one was hard
cells.intent: The version you struggle to write is a map of your own uncertainty. This is the cell people do not expect.
cells.prompt:
Looking at these five renderings, identify which was hardest to make honest and what that reveals about gaps in the underlying understanding or plan. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{renderings}}
cells.demo:
The skeptical senior engineer version is the one that could not be written confidently, and the reason is not rhetorical.

Every other version can be produced from the intent alone. That one requires you to have an actual answer to "what happens when ordering breaks and a customer is billed twice," and the version above does not have one — it has a reason to believe billing is a good place to find out, which is a different thing wearing similar clothes.

That is a real gap in the plan, not a gap in the explanation. If the honest version of your pitch to your most skeptical reader is "we think this is where the trade pays," you have a hypothesis and a schedule, and the schedule is currently more specific than the hypothesis.

The customer version being trivially easy is the confirming signal: it is easy precisely because it is the one where nothing is actually being claimed.

title: Steelman Yourself
blurb: Builds the strongest possible case against a position you hold, finds where the other side is genuinely right, and scores how much of your view survives.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: A position you hold and would defend
input.placeholder: State it as you would to someone who disagrees.
input.seed: Design systems should be owned by a central team, not federated across product teams. Federation sounds collaborative but in practice produces four versions of every component and nobody accountable for the drift.

cells.title: State it precisely
cells.intent: Most positions are less specific than their holder thinks. Precision is what makes a position falsifiable.
cells.prompt:
Restate this position as precisely as possible: what exactly is being claimed, under what conditions, and what would count as the claim being wrong. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.position}}
cells.demo:
Claim: in organisations above some size threshold, central ownership of a design system produces lower component duplication and clearer accountability for consistency than federated ownership.

Conditions left unstated in the original: the size threshold, whether "owned" means authored-by or approved-by, and whether the central team is resourced to keep up with product velocity.

It would be wrong if federated teams in comparable organisations produced equal or lower drift, or if central ownership reduced drift while producing a worse outcome elsewhere — slower product teams, or a system nobody adopts because it never fits.

cells.title: The strongest case against
cells.intent: Written by someone who wants to win, not someone being fair.
cells.prompt:
Write the strongest argument against this position, as an intelligent advocate for the opposite view. Do not hedge or balance. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{precise}}
cells.demo:
Central ownership does not eliminate drift. It relocates it, into a queue.

When a product team needs a component variant the central team has not built, they do not wait — the deadline does not move because the design system has a backlog. They build it locally and mark it as temporary. Now you have the same four versions, except three of them are undocumented, unowned, and invisible to the central team that believes it owns consistency.

Federation is usually measured against an idealised central model rather than a real one. The real one is a team of four supporting sixty, whose adoption rate is the number that actually predicts consistency — and adoption is driven by fit, which central teams are structurally worst positioned to judge.

The accountability argument is the weakest part. A central team accountable for consistency it cannot enforce is not accountability, it is blame with a roadmap. Federated ownership with a shared contract and an automated drift check gets you the same consistency with none of the queue.

cells.title: Where they are actually right
cells.intent: The concessions that cost you something. If the list is comfortable, it is not honest.
demo: **The queue is real and it was not accounted for.** The original position compares central ownership to federated chaos, not to central ownership under realistic resourcing.
**Adoption rate is the better metric than duplication count**, and the original position never mentioned it. A system with zero duplication and 30% adoption is worse than the reverse.
**"Accountable" was doing unearned work.** A central team cannot enforce consistency without either merge rights or a lint gate, and the position assumed accountability without naming the mechanism.
**Automated drift detection changes the arithmetic.** Much of the case for centralisation was really a case for visibility, and visibility can now be tooling rather than org structure.

cells.title: What survives
cells.intent: Not a winner. What is left of the original once the honest concessions are made.
cells.demo:
What survives is narrower and better: central ownership of the *contract* — the token layer, the accessibility floor, the API shape — with federated authorship of components against it.

What has to be abandoned is the claim as stated. "Design systems should be owned by a central team" does not survive, because it was never really an argument about ownership; it was an argument about drift visibility, and drift visibility turns out to be a tooling problem that centralisation solved by accident and expensively.

Restated: *the contract should be central and enforced automatically; the components should be federated and their conformance should be measured, not reviewed.* That version keeps everything the original was actually worried about and drops the part that was org-chart preference wearing an argument.

Note what happened — the concession about automated drift detection did most of the damage. The position was formed before that tooling was cheap, and had not been re-examined since.

title: Revise Until It Holds
blurb: Attacks your claim, and if it does not survive, sends the run back to restate it — up to three times. The notebook loops until the claim stops falling over.
teaches: Recursion — the notebook decides to try again

input.label: A claim you want to make stick
input.placeholder: One sentence. The stronger the better.
input.seed:
Remote work makes engineering teams less productive.
context: Said in a leadership offsite; people nodded; nobody defined productive.
want: A claim that can survive attack — or die cleanly.

cells.title: Sharpen the claim
cells.intent: Vague claims cannot fail, which is why they feel safe. This makes it specific enough to be attacked.
demoPass: Claim: engineering teams working fully remotely ship less per engineer per quarter than comparable co-located teams. Scope is unstated — team size, seniority, and domain are all unspecified, and "productive" is being measured as shipped output rather than outcome. It would be wrong if comparable remote teams matched or exceeded co-located output on the same measure.

Claim: engineering teams that moved to remote WITHOUT changing how they coordinate ship less per quarter, because the practices they relied on were co-located ones. Scope: teams above roughly eight people, in their first year after the change. Measured as cycle time from ready to merged. It would be wrong if such teams matched their own prior cycle time within a year without changing coordination practices.

cells.title: Attack it
cells.intent: The strongest available objection, written by someone who wants the claim to fall.
cells.prompt:
Write the strongest objection to this claim. Aim to break it. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{sharp}}
demoPass:
The claim confuses a change with a cause. Teams that went remote also went remote during a pandemic, changed hiring, lost people, and absorbed a macro shock — attributing the output drop to remoteness requires ruling out all of it, and the claim does not.

Worse, "productive" is doing the heavy lifting unexamined. Shipped output per engineer is the measure most sensitive to coordination overhead and least sensitive to whether the right thing was built. Plenty of co-located teams ship more of the wrong thing faster.

This is much harder to attack, because it has stopped claiming remoteness causes the drop and started claiming unchanged coordination does. That is nearly tautological — teams that do not adapt to a change do worse after it — but it is not empty, since it makes a testable prediction about the first year and about cycle time specifically.

The remaining weakness is the eight-person threshold. Nothing in the argument produces that number; it is asserted.

cells.title: Does it hold?
cells.intent: The gate. If the claim survives, the run continues. If it does not, this cell rewrites it and sends the run back to cell 01.

demoPass.reason: It does not hold. The objection identifies a confound the claim cannot rule out — remoteness arrived alongside several other changes — and the measure chosen is the one most flattering to the conclusion. As written, the claim would be defended by anyone who already believed it and dismissed by anyone who did not.
demoPass.revision: Engineering teams that moved to remote without changing how they coordinate ship less, because the practices they depended on were co-located ones — measured as cycle time, in the first year after the change.

demoPass.reason: It holds now. The revised claim survives the objection because it no longer asserts that remoteness itself causes the drop — it names unchanged coordination as the mechanism, which is testable and which the objection does not touch. The unearned eight-person threshold is a real weakness, but a weakness in precision rather than in the argument.

cells.title: What you can now say
cells.intent: Only reached once the claim survives, or once the passes run out. Either way you learn something true.
cells.demo:
What survived: teams that went remote without changing their coordination practices lost cycle time, and the cause is the unchanged practices rather than the remoteness.

What it costs you: the original claim was an argument against remote work, and this one is not. It is an argument for changing how you coordinate when the conditions change — which applies equally to a team that moves offices, doubles in size, or splits across time zones. You have traded a position people will fight you about for one they will mostly agree with, and that is usually what happens when a claim is made precise enough to test.

What it still owes: the eight-person threshold is asserted, not derived. Either find the number or drop it.

title: Pre-Mortem
blurb: Assumes the thing already failed, eighteen months from now, and works backwards to find out why. Reliably surfaces risks a forward-looking review misses.
teaches: Plan — sequence, dependency, failure

input.label: What you are about to commit to
input.placeholder: The initiative, the bet, the hire, the launch.
input.seed: We are going to build an internal AI assistant for our support team. Six months, three engineers, trained on our help centre and past tickets. Goal is to cut first-response time in half.

cells.title: It is eighteen months later. It failed.
cells.intent: Not "what could go wrong" — it already did. The certainty is what unlocks the honest answers.
cells.prompt:
It is 18 months later and this failed completely. Write the short, unsparing account of what happened, in past tense, as if it is already known. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.plan}}
cells.demo:
It shipped on time and nobody used it.

The assistant answered the questions the help centre already answered well, which were not the questions arriving in tickets. Support agents tried it for about three weeks, found that checking its answer took longer than writing their own, and quietly stopped. First-response time did not move.

By month nine the team had been reassigned. The assistant stayed up because nobody wanted to be the person who turned it off, and it slowly drifted out of date as the product changed. It is still running.

cells.title: Working backwards
cells.intent: Each cause, ranked by how early it was already true.
cells.prompt:
From this failure account, work backwards to root causes. For each give the earliest point it was already true and whether it was knowable then. Return a table: Cause, Already true by, Knowable then?. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{obit}}

rows: Training data was the help centre, but tickets are the questions the help centre failed to answer
Verification cost exceeded writing cost, so agents rationally stopped
Yes — but only if anyone had timed it
Success was measured as response time, which agents do not control alone
Yes — agents would have said so if asked
Yes — the plan funded a build, not a service
Nobody was accountable for turning it off
No — this one is a governance gap, not a foresight one

cells.title: The cheapest moment to have known
cells.intent: Of all of it, the one check that would have changed the most, done before anything is committed.
cells.prompt:
Identify the single earliest, cheapest check that would most likely have prevented this failure, and say exactly how to run it this week. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{causes}}
cells.demo:
Read fifty real tickets against the help centre, and mark each one: already answered there, answered but hard to find, or not answered at all.

That single afternoon separates the three futures. If most tickets are already answered and merely hard to find, you do not need an assistant — you need search, and it is a far smaller project. If most are not answered anywhere, an assistant trained on the help centre cannot possibly work and the whole plan is aimed at the wrong corpus. Only the middle case justifies what is proposed.

It costs one person one afternoon and it can be done before anyone is hired, scoped, or committed. Every other cause in the table is downstream of getting this wrong.

cells.title: Tripwires
cells.intent: Signals to agree on now, while it is still cheap to admit them.
demo: **Week 3 after launch: daily active agents below 40% of the team.** Adoption never recovers from a bad first fortnight; if it is low here it will be lower at week 12.
**Median time-to-verify an answer exceeds median time-to-write one.** Time it directly with five agents. This is the number that actually decides whether the tool is used.
**Fewer than 30% of answers are sent without edit.** Heavy editing means agents are using it as a rough draft, which is a different and much less valuable product than the one being funded.
**No named owner with allocated time by launch day.** Not a tripwire that fires later — check it on the day, because after that nobody will.
**Agree the shutdown criterion now, in writing.** The failure account has it running eighteen months after it stopped working, and that is the cheapest thing on this list to prevent.

title: Spec → Ambiguity Report
blurb: Finds every sentence two competent people would implement differently. The disagreements you find now are the ones you do not find in review.
teaches: Extract — pull structure out of mess

input.label: Paste the spec, or drop the file
input.placeholder: Paste it as written.
input.seed: Users should be able to export their data. The export should include all their content and be delivered quickly. Large exports may be processed in the background. Users should be notified when it is ready.

cells.title: Where two people would diverge
cells.intent: Not unclear writing — writing that is clear, and clearly means two different things.
cells.prompt:
Find every phrase that two competent engineers would implement differently. Give the phrase, the two readings, and which is more expensive. Return a table: Phrase, Reading A, Reading B. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.spec}}

rows: Everything visible to them, including shared items they do not own — a permissions problem, not an export one
Same day, asynchronous. The next sentence implies B, contradicting this one
Above a time threshold. Different code, different failure modes
A stated requirement that it must support async. "May" is doing dangerous work here
Email. Also unstated: what happens if they are offline when it completes

cells.title: The questions the spec assumes are answered
cells.intent: Not ambiguities — absences. What it never occurred to anyone to write down.
demo: **What format?** Not mentioned once. CSV, JSON and a zip of originals are three different projects.
**How long is the export available, and where does it live?** An export is a copy of everything a user has — a file nobody scoped the retention or access control for.
**Can they export twice?** Rate limiting is unstated, and this is the endpoint most attractive to abuse.
**What happens to deleted content?** Regulation may require it; users may expect it excluded. The spec takes no position.
**Is this a GDPR/portability obligation or a convenience feature?** The answer changes the deadline, the format, and who signs off — and it is the single most consequential thing not written down.

cells.title: The unambiguous version
cells.intent: Same intent, no room to diverge. This is what should have been written.
cells.demo:
**Data export**

A user can request an export of all content they authored. Content shared with them but owned by others is excluded — **TBD (Legal): does portability oblige us to include shared content?**

The export is generated asynchronously in all cases. There is no synchronous path; "quickly" is replaced by a stated target: **95% of exports available within 15 minutes**, and the user is told the estimate at request time.

Format is a single zip containing JSON for structured records and original files at original resolution. **TBD (Product): is CSV needed for spreadsheet users?**

On completion the user receives an email with a signed link, valid for **7 days**, after which the artefact is deleted. The link is single-user and does not require an active session.

One export per user per **24 hours**. A second request inside the window returns the existing artefact rather than generating a new one.

Deleted content is excluded. **TBD (Legal): retention obligations may override this.**

This is a **TBD (Product): obligation or convenience?** — if obligation, the 15-minute target and 7-day window both need Legal review before build.

title: Feedback → Patterns
blurb: Turns a pile of comments into themes, separates the signal from the loudest voice, and names what to deliberately ignore.
teaches: Extract — pull structure out of mess

input.label: Raw feedback — reviews, survey text, notes
input.placeholder: One per line is fine. Messy is fine.
input.seed:
- Setup took me three tries, the docs skip a step
- Love it once it works
- Too expensive for what it does
- I can never find the export button
- Why is there no dark mode??
- Crashed twice on large files
- The onboarding video is great
- Setup instructions assume you already have an account

Setup is the most-mentioned and it is also genuinely the most costly, which is unusual — normally the loudest theme is not the most expensive one. Three mentions in fourteen, and every one describes a user who nearly did not get in at all. Everything downstream is conditional on this.

Large file handling is the quiet expensive one. Two mentions, but one of them says "dealbreaker" and the other says "unusable" — that is not a complaint, that is a churn event that already happened and got written down politely.

**Dark mode, for now.** Real but not load-bearing. The honest reason is priority, not disagreement — say that out loud rather than letting it die silently, or it returns every quarter.
**"Too expensive for what it does."** Not actionable as stated, and price complaints are usually value-communication complaints. It belongs with the pricing-clarity theme, not with pricing.

title: The Difficult Message
blurb: Drafts something hard to say, then reads it back as the person receiving it on their worst day — and shows you which sentence does the damage.
teaches: Translate — same idea, different reader

input.label: What you need to say, and to whom
input.placeholder: The situation, plainly. You do not need to be diplomatic here.
input.seed: I need to tell a contractor we are not renewing. Their work was fine but we are bringing it in-house. They have been with us two years and I think they assume this is going to be renewed. They have not done anything wrong.

cells.title: The plain draft
cells.intent: What you actually mean, before it gets softened into something that says nothing.
cells.prompt:
Write this message directly and kindly. Lead with the decision. No euphemism, no padding. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.situation}}
cells.demo:
Hi —

I want to tell you directly rather than let you find out from a silence: we are not renewing the contract when it ends. This is not about your work, which has been consistently good. We are moving this function in-house.

I know you have been planning around this continuing, and I am sorry to be the reason that changes. I would like to give you as much runway as I can — the contract runs to the end of March, and I am happy to talk about how we use that time.

I would also like to be a reference for you, and I mean that as a specific offer rather than a polite one.

Can we talk this week?

cells.title: Read on their worst day
cells.intent: The same words, received by someone who is worried about money and half-expecting bad news.

rows: "rather than let you find out from a silence"
Implies you considered doing exactly that. Reads as a favour rather than the baseline.
The sentence everyone hears as "this is about your work." Denial before accusation invites the accusation.
Sounds cheaper and permanent. Reads as: you were the expensive stopgap.
"I know you have been planning around this continuing"
Slightly presumptuous, and reminds them of the plans they now have to unmake.
Hedged. "As I can" sounds like there is a constraint they have not been told about.
"I mean that as a specific offer"
Good — the strongest line in the message, and the only one that costs you something.

cells.title: The version that survives that reading
cells.intent: Not softer. The same decision, with the sentences that do collateral damage removed.
cells.demo:
Hi —

We are not renewing the contract when it ends in March. I wanted to tell you now so you have the most time possible.

The decision is about where the work sits, not about how it has been done. We are building the capability internally, and that was decided above this contract rather than because of it. Your work has been good and I would say so to anyone who asked.

On that: I will be a reference, and I will write it this month rather than waiting to be asked.

The contract runs to 31 March and I am not looking to shorten it. If a shorter or longer wind-down suits you better, tell me and I will try to make it work.

Can we talk this week?

cells.title: What this still costs
cells.intent: What no wording fixes. Knowing this stops you rewriting it a sixth time.
cells.demo:
They are losing income they were counting on, and no arrangement of sentences changes that. The revision removes the readings that would have added insult, which is the entire available win. It does not make the message good news and you should stop trying to.

One thing genuinely improved and it was not the wording: "I will write the reference this month rather than waiting to be asked" is a commitment with a date. The original offered to be a reference, which is what everyone says. This one can be checked.

The thing to accept: they may respond badly, and that will not mean you wrote it wrong. Two years of work ending is worth a bad reaction. Send it, then be available.

title: Why This Test Is Flaky
blurb: Separates the four reasons a test fails intermittently, then tells you which one you have — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Diagnose — find the cause, not the symptom

input.label: The test, and what you have observed
input.placeholder: Paste the test or describe it. Include how often it fails.
input.seed: An integration test for checkout fails maybe 1 in 15 runs in CI, never locally. It asserts the order total after a discount is applied. Started about three weeks ago.

cells.title: Which kind of flake
cells.intent: There are only a few. Naming yours narrows the search enormously.
cells.prompt:
Classify this flake against the standard causes — timing/async, shared state, ordering, environment, real intermittent bug. Score each. Table: Cause, Fits?, Why. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.test}}

rows: Passes alone, fails in CI where tests run together. Discounts are usually global config.
Checkout is multi-step; an unawaited write would produce exactly this rate.
Same evidence as shared state, and CI probably randomises order.
Would fail far more than 1 in 15, and would not have started three weeks ago.
1 in 15 in checkout is a customer-facing rate. This is the expensive branch.

cells.title: The experiment that separates them
cells.intent: One change that gives a different answer per cause.
cells.prompt:
Give experiments that discriminate between the remaining causes — each must produce a different result depending on which is true. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{kind}}
demo: **Run the test 200 times alone, in a loop.** Fails: not shared state. Passes: it is the neighbours.
**Pin the seed so CI runs tests in the same order every time.** If the flake becomes deterministic, it is ordering.
**Log the discount config at assertion time, not setup time.** If it differs on failures, another test is mutating it.
**Check what changed three weeks ago.** A flake with a start date has a commit. This is the cheapest step and the one most often skipped.

cells.title: Fix versus suppress
cells.intent: Retry annotations are a decision. This makes it an explicit one.
cells.demo:
Do not add a retry. Not because retries are always wrong, but because this test asserts a money value in checkout — the one place where an intermittent failure might be reporting a real intermittent bug rather than a test defect.

If the loop-200-times run passes, it is shared state and the fix is isolation: build discount config per test rather than mutating a shared object. That is an afternoon and it fixes every other test that will hit this later.

If it fails alone, you have a race in checkout that customers hit at some rate you have not measured. Retrying would hide it, and that is the outcome worth avoiding.

title: Rewrite This Error Message
blurb: Judges an error against the only three things an error owes the reader, then rewrites it — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: The error message
input.placeholder: Paste it exactly.
input.seed:
Error: Something went wrong. Please try again later. (code: ERR_UNSPECIFIED_500)
constraint: Be specific enough that two colleagues would disagree about the next step — that disagreement is the point of this notebook (The error message).

cells.title: What it owes
cells.intent: What happened, why, and what to do. Most errors deliver one.
cells.prompt:
Score this error on: says what happened, says why, says what to do next. Table: Obligation, Met?, Evidence. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.err}}

rows: A 500 code is our failure, and the message implies the user caused it.
"Try again later" is advice only if retrying could work — and nothing says it could.
The passive voice puts an internal failure on the reader.

cells.title: Three rewrites
cells.intent: One per plausible underlying cause, because a generic error is a refusal to find out.

rows: We could not reach the payment service. Nothing was charged. Try again in a minute — if it keeps failing, this is on us and support has the reference EX-4821.
Bad input we failed to validate
The card expiry date is not a real date. Check the month and year and try again.
Something failed on our side and we do not yet know what. Nothing was charged. We have logged it as EX-4821 — send that to support and they can see exactly what happened.

cells.title: The rule this suggests
cells.intent: One error is an instance. The pattern is what you fix.
cells.demo:
Every error carries a reference the user can hand to support, and every error says whether anything was charged or changed.

Those two facts do more than any amount of tone work. The first turns a dead end into a route; the second answers the question the user is actually asking, which is never "what went wrong" but "am I now in trouble."

The generic fallback stays — you will always have unknowns — but it must be the third message, not the first. Reaching for it when you do know the cause is what made the original bad.

title: What This Progression Is Doing
blurb: Reads a chord progression for its function rather than its names, then tells you why the third bar feels wrong.
teaches: Diagnose — find the cause, not the symptom

input.label: The progression, and where it feels off
input.placeholder: Chords in order. Key if you know it.
input.seed:
Key of A minor. Progression: Am – F – C – E7 – Am.
note: The E7 feels dramatic but the F before it feels like it arrives late — like the tension was supposed to start earlier.
ask: What harmonic job is each chord doing, and which one is confused?

cells.title: Function, not names
cells.intent: What each chord does to tension, regardless of what it is called.
cells.prompt:
Analyse each chord by harmonic function and its effect on tension. Table: Chord, Function, Tension. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.prog}}

rows: Zero. The reference everything else is heard against.
Lower still. This is the problem: it releases rather than builds.
Dominant with a raised third — the strongest pull in the key

cells.title: Why the third bar undoes you
cells.intent: Why the third bar undoes you. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
The tension curve is flat, flat, flatter, then a cliff. F and C are both consonant resting places, so bars two and three are the same emotional event twice — and C is actually more restful than F, so the progression relaxes just before it needs to be climbing.

The E7 then does all the work alone. That is why it reads as dramatic rather than earned: it has no ramp behind it. You are not hearing a build, you are hearing a jump-scare with a very pleasant three bars in front of it.

cells.title: Four ways out
cells.intent: Four ways out. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
demo: **Swap C for Dm.** One chord. Dm is subdominant minor — it leans toward E7 instead of resting. The curve now climbs.
**Keep C but put it first: Am - C - F - E7.** Same chords, and now the motion is home → bright → warm → pull, which rises.
**Make the third bar F/G or Fmaj7.** Keeps the colour, adds instability so it stops being a landing.
**Delay the E7 by two beats and put Bdim in front of it.** Most change, biggest payoff — the diminished chord is a ramp, and it is the classical answer to exactly this problem.

title: Translate the Mix Note
blurb: Turns "make it punchier" into an actual decision about frequency, dynamics, or arrangement — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: The note you were given
input.placeholder: In their words, not yours.
input.seed:
The client says the chorus "needs more energy" but also that it is "already too loud."
constraint: Be specific enough that two colleagues would disagree about the next step — that disagreement is the point of this notebook (The note you were given).

cells.title: What they might mean
cells.intent: Contradictory notes usually name a real problem badly.
cells.prompt:
List the plausible technical meanings behind this note, including why the contradiction may be consistent. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.note}}
demo: **The chorus is loud but not louder than the verse.** Energy is relative; if the verse is already at the ceiling there is nowhere to go, and the mix reads as flat rather than quiet.
**It is dense, not energetic.** More elements playing at once reads as busier, not bigger, and busier is fatiguing — which is what "too loud" often means.
**The transient information is gone.** Heavy limiting removes attack. The result measures loud and feels soft, which is exactly this pair of complaints.
**Nothing changes at the chorus except level.** No new register, no new rhythm, no lift. The arrangement is the problem, not the mix.

cells.title: How to tell which
cells.intent: How to tell which. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.prompt:
For each meaning give a quick check and what result confirms it. Table: Meaning, Check, Confirms if. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{decode}}

rows: Measure LUFS on verse vs chorus
Attack returns and it reads louder at the same loudness
Play verse into chorus with drums only

cells.title: What to say back
cells.intent: What to say back. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
I think those two notes are the same note, and I think you are right.

The chorus is loud but it is not *louder* — it sits about the same level as the verse, so it never lifts. My instinct is to pull the verse down rather than push the chorus up, which should give you the energy without adding volume.

I have made two versions:

- **A** — verse down 1.5 dB, chorus untouched
- **B** — same, plus the limiter eased so the drums get their attack back

Both are quieter overall and should feel bigger. If B is the one, we lose a little competitive loudness for a lot of punch, and I would take that trade — but tell me if you would not.

title: Break Your Own World
blurb: Finds the rule your setting states and the scene that violates it — then decides which one to keep — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: The rule, and roughly what happens
input.placeholder: Magic system, tech level, political constraint — plus a scene or two.
input.seed: Magic requires a blood price: any working costs the caster physical vitality proportional to the effect. A healer can mend a wound but ages doing it. In act two my protagonist levels a city wall and is tired but fine by the next chapter.

cells.title: The rules you have actually set
cells.intent: Stated, implied, and the ones your scenes assume without saying.
demo: Stated: magic costs vitality in proportion to effect.
Stated: the cost is physical and visible — the healer ages.
Implied: cost is paid immediately, since ageing is described as happening during the working.
Implied: there is no external battery — the caster is the only fuel.
Assumed by act two: cost can be survived and recovered from at scales that should be lethal.

cells.title: Where it breaks
cells.intent: Where it breaks. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
A city wall is orders of magnitude past a mended wound. If a healed cut costs visible years, a levelled wall costs a lifetime — and your protagonist is fine in a chapter.

What a careful reader concludes is not "the magic is inconsistent." It is that the cost is not real, which retroactively removes the tension from every earlier scene where it was. The healer ageing was the moment the reader agreed to take the system seriously; act two is the moment they stop.

This is the expensive kind of break, because it damages what you already spent.

cells.title: Which do you keep
cells.intent: You cannot keep both. This is the decision, with the cost of each.
cells.prompt:
Give the ways to resolve it, with what each costs the story. Table: Resolution, What it costs, Best if. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{break}}

rows: The wall nearly kills her; act three has her diminished
Rewrites your protagonist’s capability for the rest of the book
The cost is your theme — then this is not a cost, it is the point
She used an external source, established earlier
Requires planting it in act one, and weakens the "caster is the only fuel" rule
You want the set piece and can afford one exception with a name
The wall becomes something smaller — a gate, a section
The scene’s job is her resolve, not the scale
Cost scales with intent, not effect
Elegant, but rewrites the healer scene
You are early enough to change the system rather than the scene

title: Shot List From an Intent
blurb: Turns "I want it to feel lonely" into a list of decisions about lens, light, distance and time — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Plan — sequence, dependency, failure

input.label: What you want it to feel like, and what you are shooting
input.placeholder: The feeling first. Constraints second.
input.seed: Portraits of a family running a bakery that is closing after 40 years. I want it to feel like the end of something without being sentimental. One morning, available light only.

cells.title: The choices that carry the feeling
cells.intent: Each craft decision, and which way it leans for this brief.
cells.prompt:
Map the feeling onto concrete craft decisions. Table: Decision, This brief wants, Why. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}

rows: Closeness reads as intimacy, which tips into sentiment. Space reads as ending.
Wide dramatises, long flatters. Neither is honest here.
Window light, unmodified, let shadows go
Fill light is a kindness that removes the subject
Working hands look like continuity. Pauses look like the last time.
A portrait of people is about people. This is about a place losing them.
Grading it warm is the sentimentality you said you did not want

cells.title: The list
cells.intent: The list. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
demo: **Wide, from the doorway, before anyone arrives.** Empty room, ovens off, window light only. This is the frame the whole set is measured against.
**Full-length of one person at the bench, mid-room.** Not working. Standing.
**Two of them talking, shot from the far side of the room, through the pass.** The barrier is the point.
**Hands, but idle** — on a bench, in a pocket. Working hands are the cliché.
**A wall detail with 40 years on it.** A rota, a burn mark, a taped note.
**The group, arranged, looking at camera, from far enough back that the room wins.** Take it early. It is the one they will want.
**The doorway again at the end of the morning.** Same frame, people in it. Pair with the first.

cells.title: Shots not to take
cells.intent: Naming the clichés so you notice yourself reaching for them.
demo: **Flour in the air, backlit.** Beautiful, and it is a photo about bread. You are not photographing bread.
**A single tear or a hand on a shoulder.** If it happens, it happens — but going looking for it is how you get sentiment.
**Tight close-up of a lined face.** Reads as reverence, which flattens a person into a symbol.
**The "closed" sign.** Too literal. The room already says it.

title: Where the Tolerance Went
blurb: Stacks the errors in an assembly to find which single dimension is eating your fit — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Diagnose — find the cause, not the symptom

input.label: The assembly and the symptom
input.placeholder: Parts, nominal dimensions, tolerances, and what goes wrong.
input.seed: A three-part enclosure: base, gasket, lid. Bolts through all three. About one in eight units the lid will not seat flat and the gasket extrudes. Base flatness ±0.15, gasket thickness 2.0 ±0.1, lid flange ±0.1, bolt hole position ±0.2.

cells.title: The stack
cells.intent: Worst-case and statistical, because they disagree and the disagreement is informative.
cells.prompt:
Build the tolerance stack. Give each contributor, its range, and its share of the total. Table: Contributor, Range, Share. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.assembly}}

rows: 36% — and it acts in-plane, not in the stack

cells.title: The one that is not like the others
cells.intent: A stack tells you the size. This tells you the mechanism.
cells.demo:
One in eight is the tell. A pure stack-up failure would be far rarer — worst case needs every contributor at its limit in the same direction, which at these tolerances is a fraction of a percent. One in eight means something is not random.

Bolt hole position is the suspect, and not because it is the biggest. It is the only contributor acting in-plane. If holes are off-position, the bolts pull the lid sideways as they tighten, and the gasket extrudes because it is being sheared rather than compressed. That produces a bimodal result — fine or clearly bad, no middle — which matches a 1-in-8 rate far better than a smooth distribution would.

Check whether failures cluster by fixture or by shift. If they do, it is position, and the fix is upstream of every tolerance on this list.

cells.title: Cheapest effective change
cells.intent: Tightening everything is the expensive answer. This is the ordered one.
demo: **Clearance the lid holes by 0.5 mm.** Costs a drill change. Removes the in-plane constraint entirely and lets the gasket compress instead of shear.
**Specify a tightening sequence and torque.** Free. Cross-pattern tightening on an unsequenced assembly is a common cause of exactly this.
**Measure 30 units and plot the failures against fixture.** Costs an hour and tells you whether the above is right before you change anything.
**Tighten base flatness to ±0.08.** Real money, real machining time, and it addresses 27% of a stack that is probably not your problem. Last, not first.

title: What Is Wrong With This Plant
blurb: Works from the pattern of damage rather than the plant, which is how you tell water from disease from pests.
teaches: Diagnose — find the cause, not the symptom

input.label: What you see, and where on the plant
input.placeholder: Which leaves, what pattern, how fast, plus watering and light.
input.seed: Tomato in a raised bed. Lower leaves yellowing between the veins, working upward slowly over two weeks. Some brown spots with a yellow halo on the worst leaves. Watering daily, full sun, fed once at planting six weeks ago.

cells.title: Read the pattern, not the plant
cells.intent: Where and in what order tells you more than what it looks like.
cells.prompt:
Analyse the distribution and progression of symptoms and what each pattern implies. Table: Observation, Implies, Rules out. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.symptoms}}

rows: A mobile nutrient being withdrawn from old growth to feed new
Most fungal issues start opportunistically, not bottom-up
Yellowing between veins, veins staying green
Magnesium or nitrogen — interveinal is classic Mg
Overwatering, which yellows whole leaves uniformly
A secondary fungal issue on already-weakened tissue
Nothing — but it is likely a consequence, not the cause
Tomatoes in a bed are heavy feeders and that is long past

cells.title: Most to least likely
cells.intent: Most to least likely. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
demo: **Magnesium deficiency — most likely.** Interveinal, bottom-up, slow, six weeks unfed. Confirm: Epsom salts foliar spray; new growth greens within a week if right.
**Nitrogen deficiency — close second, often alongside.** Confirm: yellowing is more uniform than interveinal on the oldest leaves.
**Early blight — secondary.** The halo spots fit, but blight starting bottom-up on stressed lower leaves is a passenger here, not the driver.

**Overwatering — worth checking, unlikely as stated.** Daily in a raised bed in full sun is usually fine, but check drainage. Root problems mimic deficiency because the roots cannot take nutrients up.

cells.title: What to do this week
cells.intent: What to do this week. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
demo: **Remove the spotted leaves and bin them, not compost.** Stops the secondary issue spreading while you fix the cause.
**Feed with a balanced tomato feed, and add Epsom salts** — a tablespoon in 4 litres, watered in. Both deficiencies covered without guessing between them.
**Mulch.** Splash from soil onto lower leaves is how the fungal spots got there.
**Then wait a week and look at NEW growth only.** Damaged leaves never recover, and judging by them will make you think the fix failed.
**Do not spray a fungicide yet.** The spots are a symptom of a hungry plant. Fix the feeding and they usually stop appearing.

title: Why Scaling Broke It
blurb: Finds which ingredient does not scale linearly — usually salt, leavening, or time — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Diagnose — find the cause, not the symptom

input.label: The recipe, the scale factor, and what went wrong
input.seed: Doubled a brownie recipe for a party. Same tin size doubled up to a bigger tin. Came out dense and slightly bitter, and the edges were overdone while the middle was raw.
input.placeholder: What you scaled and how it failed.

cells.title: What does not scale
cells.intent: Most ingredients double. A few emphatically do not.
cells.prompt:
Identify what does not scale linearly here and why. Table: Element, Scales?, Consequence. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.recipe}}

rows: Doubled soda in a brownie gives a soapy bitterness and a cakey crumb — this is your bitter note
Roughly linear, but perception is not
Tastes stronger in a denser bake
Not linear at all — governed by depth, not volume
A deeper tin needs longer at a LOWER temperature
Depth is the variable that matters
Doubling volume in a deeper tin is the actual cause of raw middle and burnt edge

cells.title: The actual cause
cells.intent: The actual cause. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
Depth, not quantity. Heat travels inward from every surface, so bake time scales with the *thickness* of the batter, not its volume. A tin that is twice the volume but also deeper needs substantially longer — and at a lower temperature, or the outside is finished long before the middle starts.

That single change produces both symptoms at once: burnt edges and raw centre are what happens when you give a thicker bake the same time and temperature as a thinner one.

The doubled leavening explains the bitterness separately, and the density is downstream of both — underbaked centre plus over-risen-then-collapsed crumb.

cells.title: How to run it again
cells.intent: How to run it again. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
demo: **Use two tins of the original size, not one bigger one.** Same depth, same time, same temperature. This is the whole fix and it costs nothing.
**If you must use one tin: drop the oven 15°C and add 10–15 minutes**, then test the centre rather than the timer.
**Scale leavening by about 1.5×, not 2×.** For most bakes this is close enough and avoids the soapy note.
**Scale salt fully.** It is not the problem, and under-salting a doubled bake is how you get flat-tasting brownies.
**Test with a skewer at the true centre and one third of the way in.** Two readings tell you whether it is depth or temperature.

Assess against the standard plateau causes: under-recovery, under-eating, technique breakdown at load, and programme exhaustion. Table: Cause, Evidence for, Fix direction. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.plateau}}

2.5kg a session cannot continue indefinitely for anyone
Change structure — this is normal and expected
Note that the first three all say "back off" and the fourth says "change"
They are not the same instruction

cells.intent: Which one is yours. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
Sleep. Six hours with elevated work stress is the answer, and everything else here is a passenger.

Linear progression ending at seven weeks is completely normal and would have happened anyway — but it ends *earlier* and *harder* when recovery is short. Flat bodyweight while training four days a week says you are also eating at maintenance, which compounds it.

The unwelcome part: no programme change fixes this. You can restructure the training and you will get another few weeks, then stall again lower. The variable that is actually limiting you is not in the gym.

cells.title: What to change, in order
cells.intent: Ordered by effect, which is not the same as ordered by appeal.
demo: **Sleep, for two weeks, before changing anything else.** Seven and a half hours minimum. If the squat moves on that alone, you have your answer and you saved yourself a programme rewrite.
**Drop to three sessions.** Counterintuitive and correct. Four sessions on six hours sleep is four sessions of accumulating fatigue.
**Eat 200–300 kcal above maintenance.** Flat weight while progressing is only sustainable early.
**Then, and only then, change the programme.** Stop adding 2.5kg a session; move to weekly progression or a wave. This is the fun part and it is fourth for a reason.
**Film a set at 110kg.** Cheap, and rules out technique in one video.

title: Find the Hole in What You Know
blurb: Asks you to explain something, then locates the exact sentence where your understanding stops — then leaves you with a concrete next step you can take without re-reading the model output.
teaches: Teach — find the gap in your own understanding

input.label: Explain something you think you understand
input.placeholder: Write it as if to a colleague. Do not look anything up.
input.seed: A database index makes queries faster because it stores a sorted copy of the column, so the database can jump straight to the row instead of scanning the whole table.

cells.title: What you actually have
cells.intent: The parts that are correct, stated back precisely.
demo: Correct: an index is a separate structure, not a property of the table.
Correct: it is ordered, and the ordering is what enables the speedup.
Correct: the alternative is a scan, and avoiding the scan is the point.
Correct in effect: lookups become roughly logarithmic rather than linear.

cells.title: The edge of it
cells.intent: The precise sentence where the explanation stops being load-bearing.
cells.demo:
"Jump straight to the row" is where it stops.

The explanation knows the index is sorted and knows that helps, but it does not say *how* sorted data is searched — which means it cannot answer why an index on a low-cardinality column (a boolean, say) is often useless, or why range queries behave differently from equality ones, or why the query planner sometimes ignores an index you built.

The question that exposes it: **why is an index on a column with two possible values usually worse than no index at all?** If the answer is "because it still has to jump," the model is a lookup table rather than a tree, and the gap is B-trees and selectivity.

cells.title: The one thing to learn next
cells.intent: Not a syllabus. The single concept that unlocks the rest.
cells.demo:
Selectivity.

Not B-trees — that is the mechanism, and you can hold it later. Selectivity is the idea that an index is only worth using when it eliminates most of the rows, and it is the concept that makes every confusing index behaviour suddenly obvious.

Once you have it: low-cardinality indexes are useless because they eliminate half the table at best. The planner ignores your index because it estimated poor selectivity. Composite index column order matters because the most selective column should come first. Range queries differ because they eliminate less than equality does.

One idea, four mysteries. Learn that before the tree structure, not after.

1. What does "making good" cover — is that plastered and painted, or prepared for me to decorate?
2. Electrics are excluded — are you arranging a certified electrician, or am I? And where do they sit in the sequence?

4. If you open the wall and find something unexpected, what is the rate, and can we agree that anything over £200 gets a call before it happens?

title: Is This Actually Testable
blurb: Checks whether a hypothesis could ever come out false, which is the only property that makes testing it worthwhile.
teaches: Critique — attack it before reality does

input.label: The hypothesis and how you plan to test it
input.placeholder: What you think is true, and the study or experiment.
input.seed:
Hypothesis: our onboarding redesign improves user engagement.
Test: compare engagement metrics for 3 weeks pre/post for users who saw the new flow.
Worry: We called it an A/B but the assignment was messy and "engagement" means three different dashboards.

cells.title: What result would refute it
cells.intent: If you cannot state one, you are not testing anything.
cells.prompt:
State precisely what observation would falsify this hypothesis as written, and whether the proposed test could produce it. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.hyp}}
cells.demo:
As written, nothing would refute it — and that is the problem.

"Engagement" is unspecified, so any metric that moved up can be nominated afterwards as the one that mattered. If sessions fall but session length rises, the hypothesis survives. If both fall, "engagement" can become retention. A hypothesis that survives every outcome is not a hypothesis.

The before/after design compounds it: 30 days before versus 30 days after cannot separate the redesign from seasonality, a marketing push, a pricing change, or the simple fact that the users in each window are different people.

cells.title: What else could produce the result
cells.intent: Each alternative explanation, and whether the design excludes it.

rows: Compare same period year-on-year, or randomise
Measure at 7, 30 and 90 days — novelty decays
Check the release log for the window
If the redesign was triggered by a bad month, expect improvement regardless

cells.title: The version worth running
cells.intent: The version worth running. This cell exists so the next one has something sharp to work with — not a summary for its own sake.
cells.demo:
**Hypothesis.** New users randomised to the redesigned onboarding complete their first meaningful action within 7 days at a higher rate than users on the existing flow.

**Primary metric.** Percentage completing first meaningful action within 7 days. One metric, named in advance.

**Falsified if.** The redesigned group performs at or below control, or the difference is smaller than 3 percentage points.

**Design.** Randomised at signup, 50/50, running concurrently — which removes seasonality, release-log contamination, and traffic-mix effects in one move.

**Duration.** Until 2,000 users per arm, decided before starting rather than when the numbers look good.

**Secondary, exploratory, not confirmatory.** 30- and 90-day retention, to catch novelty decay.

The change that matters is not the wording. It is running the two flows *concurrently* instead of sequentially — that alone removes five of the six alternatives in the table.

**What we agreed**

**Tone.** Gritty by default, comedy welcome between scenes. If someone says "let me have this one," we stay in the scene. Anyone can say it, including me.

**Off the table.** [List what people named.] No discussion needed, ever.

cells.title: Tomorrow's open
cells.intent: The exact words you say after taking attendance.
cells.demo: Before we review last week: write one sentence — did camouflage in moths appear because soot arrived, or was it already in the population? Do not use the words need, want, or try. I am not grading correctness yet — I am listening for the model you brought in the door.

title: Does This Question Test That
blurb: Pressure-tests an exam question against the thinking skill you claim to measure, shows what it actually rewards, and rewrites it until a student cannot pass by pattern-matching.

input.label: Target construct and the exam question
input.placeholder: Name the thinking skill, paste the question, and note the course level.
input.seed:
targetConstruct: Causal reasoning — can the student distinguish correlation claims from causal claims and name a confound.
examQuestion: "Define independent variable."
course: Intro research methods, week 3.
whyYouWroteIt: Fast to grade; shows they did the reading.

cells.title: What it actually tests
cells.intent: Separate the claimed construct from the behavior that earns points.
cells.prompt:
State what thinking this question actually rewards, versus the target construct. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: It rewards definition recall. A student can define "independent variable" perfectly and still confuse correlation with causation on every applied item. The target construct — causal reasoning — is not touched.

cells.title: Validity critique
cells.intent: Where the question leaks, cues, or lets pattern-matching through.

cols: How a weak student still scores

cells.title: Rewrite candidates
cells.intent: Three questions that actually require the construct.
demo: A study finds ice cream sales and drowning rise together. Give one causal claim someone might make, and one confound that breaks it.
Researchers randomize a study app to half a class and compare final grades. What is the independent variable, and what causal claim is now more defensible than in an observational version?
"Students who sit in front get higher grades." Is this causal? If not, name a confound and one design change that would test the causal version.

cells.title: Pick the replacement
cells.intent: Choose the one you will put on the exam — cost is grading time and cueing risk.

options.label: Ice cream / drowning confound item
options.note: Classic; some students have seen it.

options.label: Randomized study-app item
options.note: Ties IV definition to causal warrant.

options.label: Front-row grades item
options.note: Closest to student life; high diagnostic value.

cells.title: Scoring key
cells.intent: What earns full credit — so you do not reintroduce memory theatre at grading time.
cells.demo:
### Full
Names a non-causal reading, a concrete confound, and a design change that addresses it.
### Half
Names confound without design change, or design without confound.
### Zero
Restates the correlation as causal, or defines terms without application.

title: Where the Field Disagrees
