input.label: Topic, starting read, and what you suspect is smoothed
input.placeholder: Name the topic, the intro chapter/article, and the disagreement you think is being papered over.
input.seed:
topic: Theories of consciousness
startingRead: Intro chapter presenting Global Workspace Theory and IIT as two "leading accounts," each with a tidy paragraph, ending on "research continues."
suspicion: The chapter never says what would falsify either, or why some researchers call IIT unfalsifiable.
reader: Advanced undergrad starting a seminar paper.

cells.title: The smoothed story
cells.intent: What the intro wants you to believe is settled.
cells.prompt:
Summarize the consensus story the starting read sells — and what questions it quietly declines to ask. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: The chapter sells a two-horse race: GWT vs IIT, both serious, both ongoing. It declines to ask what evidence would retire either horse, how "information integration" is measured without circularity, or why parts of the field treat the dispute as methodological rather than empirical.

cells.title: Dispute inventory
cells.intent: Live disagreements with stakes — not vibe disagreements.
demo: Falsifiability of IIT — is Φ a scientific quantity or a restatement of the phenomenon?
Whether GWT explains phenomenology or only reportability and access.
Whether NCC searches assume a theory of consciousness they claim to test.
How much "leading account" status is citation politics versus predictive success.

cells.title: Reading that exposes the fight
cells.intent: A short stack that makes disagreement primary, not a footnote.

rows: IIT primer + a sharp critique (e.g. unfalsifiability arguments)
Methods paper on NCC identification problems

title: What This Method Cannot See
blurb: Bounds a method against the question you want answered, tables the blind spots as if they were features, and upgrades the next design instead of overclaiming the current one.
teaches: Diagnose — methods fail silently when the question outruns them

input.label: Method and the question you hope it can answer
input.placeholder: Name the method, the research question, and any constraints (time, access, ethics).
input.seed:
method: Cross-sectional survey of knowledge workers (n≈400), self-reported innovation behaviors.
question: Does remote work improve team innovation?
constraint: Six weeks, no experimental assignment, company will not share performance data.
temptation: Report correlations as "impact of remote work."

cells.title: Bound the method
cells.intent: What it can warrant — said tightly enough that overclaim becomes obvious.
cells.prompt:
State what causal or descriptive claims this method can actually support for this question. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: At best: associations between reported remoteness and reported innovation behaviors in this sample, at one time, with all the usual self-report bias. It cannot warrant "remote work improves team innovation" — no temporal order, no assignment, no team-level outcome, no handling of who gets to be remote.

cells.title: Blind spot table
cells.intent: Each blind spot as a failure mode, not a caveat footnote.

rows: Innovative teams may win remote flexibility

cells.title: Next-method upgrade
cells.intent: The smallest design change that buys a real warrant — given the constraints.
demo: Add a prior-wave or archival date of remote start → weak temporal order; still not causal.
Replace self-report innovation with counted shipped experiments / patents / RFCs → better outcome, still observational.
Compare matched teams differing in remote policy with difference-in-differences if a policy change exists → closer to causal.
If no design upgrade is possible: rewrite the question to "how do remote workers describe innovation practices" and stop.

cells.title: Claim you will publish
cells.intent: Force the honest title — the capability is refusing the tempting one.

options.label: Associations between remoteness and reported innovation practices
options.note: Matches the method.

options.label: Remote work and innovation: correlational evidence
options.note: Borderline; needs loud limitations.

options.label: Remote work improves team innovation
options.note: Unsupported — include only as the trap option.

cells.title: Limitations paragraph
cells.intent: Write it now — before results tempt you to soften it.
cells.demo: This cross-sectional self-report survey cannot identify the effect of remote work on team innovation. Remoteness is not randomly assigned; innovation is not observed in behavior; and reverse causality remains plausible. Readers should treat associations as descriptive of this sample's reports, not as a mandate for workplace policy.

title: Explain It at Three Depths
blurb: Renders one idea for three audiences via a map, then checks which depth you cannot write — that gap is where your own understanding is thin.
teaches: Translate — the depth you cannot write is the depth you do not have

input.label: Idea and the three audiences
input.placeholder: Name the idea and three readers from shallow to deep.
input.seed:
idea: Bayes' theorem — updating a belief when new evidence arrives.
audiences: middle-school student; undergrad who has seen fractions but not formal probability; domain researcher who uses p-values casually and distrusts "Bayesian" as branding.
goal: Find which depth I am faking.

cells.title: Depth ladder
cells.intent: What each audience is allowed to not know — and what they must still leave with.
cells.prompt:
Define three depth targets: what each audience must leave understanding, and what jargon is forbidden. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
demo: Middle school: beliefs can get stronger or weaker when new facts arrive; no formulas.
Undergrad: prior × likelihood → posterior intuition with a simple numeric example; minimal notation.
Researcher: when Bayesian updating changes a decision versus when it is theatre; address p-value habits directly.

cells.title: Depth mapping
cells.intent: One pass per audience — map forces coverage instead of one middle-altitude waffle.
cells.prompt:
For {{audience}}, explain the idea at that depth. Keep it self-contained. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
demo: Middle school: You thought your friend usually texts back fast. Today they did not. That new fact should change how sure you are they are free — not prove anything alone.
Undergrad: Start with a prior odds. Multiply by how many times more likely the evidence is under one hypothesis than the other. The result is your new odds — a number you can show on paper.
Researcher: If your decision threshold would not move under any plausible likelihood ratio from this study, the Bayesian language is costume. If it would move, write the prior you are actually using.

cells.title: Where you are thin
cells.intent: Which depth was hardest to write — that is the diagnosis.
cells.demo: The researcher depth is the thinnest if it stays slogan-level about p-values without a concrete decision threshold. Study: take one paper you like, write the prior odds you actually had, and compute whether the likelihood ratio should have moved your next experiment. If you cannot, you do not yet own Bayes at that altitude.

title: Show the Thinking, Not the Answer
blurb: Takes a worked problem and a common error, rebuilds the reasoning steps a learner should see, and adds error-proof checks that catch the mistake before the final number.
teaches: Teach — answers hide the moves students need to steal

input.label: Problem, correct approach, and common error
input.placeholder: Paste the problem, what good thinking looks like, and the wrong move students make.
input.seed:
problem: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours, then 90 km in 3 hours. What is average speed for the whole trip?
commonError: Average the two speeds (60 and 30) to get 45 km/h.
correct: Total distance / total time = 210/5 = 42 km/h.
whyItMatters: The error is a concept error about what "average" means for rates, not arithmetic.

cells.title: The wrong move named
cells.intent: Name the mistaken concept — not "they forgot the formula."
cells.prompt:
Name the conceptual error in the common wrong approach. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: Students treat average speed as the average of speeds, as if each segment counted equally regardless of time. They are averaging rates without weighting by time — a category error about what the average is an average of.

cells.title: Worked steps
cells.intent: Visible moves a learner can steal — including the check that rejects 45.

rows: Forces the numerator of the real average
Forces the denominator — time is the weight
Makes the wrong concept fail out loud

cells.title: Error-proof checks
cells.intent: Questions that catch the mistake before the box is filled.
demo: Before averaging any rates: "Am I weighting by time, or treating segments as equal votes?"
Units check: does my answer have distance/time for the whole trip?
Sanity: if more time was spent slow, average should sit closer to the slow speed — 42 is closer to 30 than 45 is.
Explain without numbers: average speed is total distance over total time — say it before calculating.

title: Questions Before the Appointment
blurb: Turns a vague worry and a short visit into a prioritized question list, a what-to-ask-if-there's-time tier, and a record template so you leave with answers instead of adrenaline.
teaches: Plan — scarce clinical time rewards prepared questions

input.label: Visit type, symptoms, and constraints
input.placeholder: What the visit is for, what you need answered, and how long you get.
input.seed:
visit: 15-minute primary care follow-up.
symptoms: Fatigue for 6 weeks, headaches after lunch, sleep fragmented (wake 3–4am).
alreadyTried: Iron-rich food, earlier bedtime, caffeine cut after 2pm — no clear change.
fear: Being told "it's stress" without a plan.
mustLearn: What to rule out, what to track for 2 weeks, when to escalate.

cells.title: What must be answered
cells.intent: If the visit ends and these are unanswered, it failed — regardless of bedside manner.
cells.prompt:
State the must-answer questions for this visit, given the time constraint. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: Must answer: (1) Which serious causes are we ruling out first, and how? (2) What should I track for two weeks that would change the next step? (3) What is the escalate-sooner trigger — symptom, severity, or timeline?

cells.title: Prioritized ask list
cells.intent: Order for a 15-minute clock — first questions earn the right to later ones.
demo: MUST: Given fatigue + fragmented sleep + afternoon headaches, what are the top three causes you want to rule out in what order?
MUST: What should I log for 14 days that would change your next recommendation?
MUST: What change would make you want me back sooner than the routine follow-up?
IF TIME: Could medications, iron, thyroid, or apnea screening be relevant — and what is the cheapest first check?
IF TIME: If this is stress-mediated, what is the concrete plan — not just the label?

cells.title: Leave-with template
cells.intent: Fill-in lines so answers become a record, not a memory.

rows: Stops the loop of vague reassurance

title: Repair or Replace
blurb: Frames the broken thing against remaining life, forces a repair / replace / live-with choice with cost, and leaves a next-action card that includes the failure mode if you guess wrong.
teaches: Compare — the cheap repair is expensive when it fails twice

input.label: Broken thing, quotes, and constraints
input.placeholder: What failed, age, repair vs replace quotes, and how long you can live without it.
input.seed:
appliance: 8-year-old dishwasher; intermittent leak at door seal, sometimes puddles by morning.
quotes: Repair (seal+labor) $280; mid replacement $780 installed; open-box unit $620.
history: Same seal repaired 18 months ago for $190.
constraint: Kitchen is primary; can hand-wash for ~5 days max before it becomes a fight.
uncertainty: Tech says "probably seal" but won't warrant against a hidden pump issue.

cells.title: Decision frame
cells.intent: Remaining life, second-failure cost, and downtime — before money feelings take over.
cells.prompt:
Frame repair vs replace using age, prior repairs, downtime tolerance, and second-failure cost. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: At eight years with a repeat seal repair, you are paying again for a failure mode that already returned. Repair is rational only if you accept a real chance of a second bill inside a year. Replacement costs more now but resets the clock; hand-wash tolerance is five days, so either path needs scheduling, not hope.

cells.title: Select a path
cells.intent: Repair, replace, or live-with — cost includes the second failure.

options.label: Repair seal now ($280)
options.note: Only if you can absorb another failure within a year.

options.label: Replace (open-box $620 or mid $780)
options.note: Best when prior repair already failed once.

options.label: Live with it 30 days + catch pans
options.note: Only to buy time for a sale — set a hard end date.

cells.title: Next actions
cells.intent: Calendar the path — including what you do if the guess is wrong.
demo: If replace: measure bay + water line today; order unit with delivery ≤5 days; keep old unit until first cycle succeeds.
If repair: get written "if not seal, diagnosis fee applies" in quote; book within 48 hours.
If live-with: put a hard calendar date 30 days out; catch pans + humidity check each morning.
Either paid path: photograph leak area before work for warranty disputes.

title: Read a Screenshot
blurb: Show it a picture of a screen and it says what a first-time arrival actually does with it — in order, and where they stop.
teaches: Vision — the notebook can see what you show it

input.label: A screenshot of the screen you are worried about
input.placeholder: Say what the screen is for, and who arrives at it.
input.seed: A signup screen for a small team analytics tool. Most people arrive from a link in a colleague's message and have never heard of us.
input.seedAlt: Sample signup screen: email, workspace URL, company size, consent, Continue

cells.title: Say what is on the screen
cells.intent: Inventory before judgement. Most disagreements about a design are really disagreements about what is there.
cells.prompt:
Look at the attached picture of an interface. List every distinct element you can see — controls, labels, blocks of text, images — in reading order. Describe only what is there. Do not evaluate it, do not suggest anything. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

What the sender says this screen is: {{input.shot}}
demo: A header bar with a small square mark and a wordmark, and one circular control at the far right.
A heading: “Create your workspace”.
A line under it: “Free for 14 days. No card needed.”
A field labelled “Work email”, empty.
A field labelled “Workspace URL”, empty, with a fixed grey block reading “.acme.app” attached to its right.
A field labelled “Company size”, showing “Select…” with a downward chevron.
An unchecked checkbox beside three lines of small print covering terms, a data processing addendum, an acceptable use policy, and consent to marketing email.
A full-width filled button: “Continue”.
Two lines of small text below: “Already have an account?” and “Single sign-on”, neither visibly a link.

cells.title: Walk the first minute
cells.intent: A screen is not read, it is worked through. Putting the order on a clock is what makes the stall visible.
cells.prompt:
Here is an inventory of a screen. Walk through what a first-time visitor does, in order, from arrival to either finishing or giving up. Use elapsed time as the “when”. Be concrete about attention: what they look at, what they skip. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{seen}}

events.what: Reads the heading, decides this is the right place
events.why: “Create your workspace” matches the promise in the colleague's message.

events.what: Types a work email without hesitating
events.why: The only field on the screen whose answer they already have.

events.what: Stops at Workspace URL
events.why: Nothing says whether this is public, whether it can be changed later, or whether their colleague already made one.

events.what: Types the company name, sees it is taken or is not sure
events.why: There is no availability feedback in the picture, so the field gives nothing back.

events.what: Opens Company size and picks the nearest bracket
events.why: Fast, but they cannot tell why it is being asked or whether it changes the price.

events.what: Skips the three lines of small print and ticks the box
events.why: Consent to marketing is bundled with the terms, so the box is the only way forward.

events.what: Presses Continue
events.why: Or leaves — the two people most likely to leave never got past the URL field.

cells.title: Name where they stop, and what it costs
cells.intent: The value is not a list of improvements. It is which single moment loses the most people, and what the cheapest true fix is.
cells.prompt:
From this walkthrough, list the moments where a real person hesitates or leaves. For each: the moment, why it happens, roughly how many are lost there compared with the others (high / some / few), and the smallest change that would actually fix it — not a redesign. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{path}}

rows: An irreversible-looking public name asked before any value has been shown
Fill it from the email domain and let it be changed later
Reads as sales qualification, and its consequence is unstated
Move it after signup, or say why it is asked
Marketing email is tied to the terms, so agreeing feels like a trick
Split into two checkboxes; only the terms are required
Not styled as a link, so people arriving from a work account do not see the fast path
Make it a button of equal weight to Continue

title: Moodboard from a Brief
blurb: Turns a written brief into a stated visual direction and then draws it — twice, in two honestly different directions, so you are choosing rather than accepting.
teaches: Image generation — the notebook draws, and says what it was going for

input.label: The brief, in whatever state it is in
input.placeholder: What is being made, for whom, and the feeling it should carry.
input.seed: Launch page for a small-batch coffee roaster shipping direct. Buyers are people who already grind at home and are bored of subscription branding. It should feel like a workshop, not a start-up. Warm, unhurried, a bit imperfect.

cells.title: State one visual direction
cells.intent: A prompt written before a direction is stated is a wish. This is the sentence the pictures have to be judged against.
cells.prompt:
Read this brief and state ONE visual direction in a single dense paragraph a drawing model can work from: subject, composition, medium, palette with named colours, lighting, and the feeling. No lists, no headings, no hedging. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.brief}}
cells.demo: A still life photographed on a worn workshop bench in late afternoon: an open kraft bag of beans spilling a little, a battered hand grinder, a single cup with a chipped rim, and a strip of masking tape with a hand-written roast date. Warm side light raking in from the left, long soft shadows, dust in the air. Palette of amber, scorched umber, deep pine green and unbleached paper. Shot slightly from above at an angle, generous empty space at the top right for a headline. Nothing new-looking, nothing symmetrical, nothing centred.

cells.title: State a direction that disagrees with it
cells.intent: Two options one degree apart is a formality. This one is required to disagree, so the choice is real.
cells.demo: A hard-edged graphic composition rather than a photograph: a cold dark ground, an exact grid, a single pale rectangle carrying the product name, one saturated aqua block for the roast marker, and a thin circle floating clear of the grid. Flat colour, no texture, no shadow, everything aligned to the grid except one deliberate break. Palette of near-black, bone white and one aqua. Precision as the message — this roaster measures things — which is the opposite argument to warmth and worth seeing before it is dismissed.

cells.title: Draw the first direction
cells.intent: Reading a direction and looking at it are different judgements. This is the one that settles it.
cells.prompt: {{direction}}

demo.alt: Warm workshop moodboard: amber arc over a burnt-umber ground, dark uprights, palette swatches along the base

cells.title: Draw the one that disagrees
cells.intent: Same brief, same care, opposite argument. Put them side by side and the brief usually turns out to have been two briefs.
cells.prompt: {{alt}}

demo.alt: Cold graphic moodboard: exact grid on near-black, pale block, aqua marker, thin circle off the grid

cells.title: What to look at when you choose
cells.intent: Left alone, people pick the prettier picture. These are the questions that make it a decision about the brief instead.
demo: Which one still reads as this roaster if the logo is removed — and which becomes any brand in the category?
Which one survives being printed on a kraft bag at 3 cm, badly?
The brief said workshop, not start-up. Which one would a start-up have chosen?
Which one can carry a headline without the headline fighting the image?
Which one will still be true in a year, when the range has doubled and half of it is not warm?

title: Redraw It
blurb: Attaches a sketch, reads it back to you in words, then draws the version you asked for — so you can see exactly which words did the work.
teaches: A picture in, a picture out, and the sentence in between

input.placeholder: Attach the drawing. In the note, say what should be different.
input.seed: Make it a clean straight-on drawing with the dimensions decided rather than questioned. Keep the three legs and the oak. Seat at 320 across, 450 high.
input.seedAlt: Rough pencil sketch of a three-legged stool with unresolved dimensions

cells.title: Read the drawing back
cells.intent: Everything downstream is built on this sentence. If the reading is wrong you will see it here, in words, before anything is redrawn.
cells.prompt:
Describe the attached drawing exactly as it is: what the object is, its parts, proportions, the marks and annotations on it, and anything left undecided. Plain prose, no judgement, no suggestions. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

What the person wants changed, for context only — do not apply it yet: {{input.piece}}
cells.demo: A quick pencil sketch of a three-legged stool, drawn in loose double lines so every edge is two strokes. A round seat seen slightly from above, with a rim suggested underneath. Three tapered legs splaying outward, and a curved stretcher joining them roughly two thirds of the way down. Two dimension lines are pencilled in red: the height is marked “45? 48?” and the seat width “about 32 across” — both unresolved. A note at the top left reads “three-leg stool”, and under it “oak offcuts · no screws showing”. Nothing is squared up and the leg angles are not consistent between the two sides.

cells.title: Write the drawing brief
cells.intent: The change is made here, in a sentence you can argue with — not inside the drawing model where you cannot see it.
cells.demo: A clean straight-on product drawing of a three-legged oak stool on a plain warm ground, flat even light, no perspective drama and no sketchy line work. Round seat 320 mm across with a softened edge and a visible underside rim; three tapered legs splaying gently outward to 450 mm overall height; a curved stretcher joining all three legs about two thirds down. Oak throughout, warm mid-brown with the grain visible, joints clean and no fixings showing. Dimension lines in a quiet grey along the right edge and the base, labelled 450 and 320 seat. Resolved, calm and buildable — the drawing a maker would pin to the wall, not the one they scribbled.

cells.title: Draw it
cells.intent: Same object, decisions made. If it comes back wrong, the brief above is the thing to edit — which is the whole point of writing it down.
cells.prompt: {{brief}}

title: Lay Out a Room

input.label: The room, and what has to go in it
input.placeholder: Dimensions if you have them, and where the doors and windows are.
input.seed: Living room 4.6 m by 3.4 m, 2.5 m ceiling. Door in the middle of one short wall, window filling most of the opposite short wall. Needs: three-seat sofa, two armchairs, a low table, a floor lamp, and shelves for about 60 books. Two adults, one cat, no television.

{{input.room}}

0.40 m to turn into; angled, not squared to a wall
0.40–0.45 m from the sofa — nearer and it blocks, further and it is useless
0.75 m standing room; not across the window wall
Beside a seat, on the side away from the window
Must stay clear end to end — assumed, not stated

cells.title: Put it in the room
cells.intent: Positions as numbers, not adjectives. You can turn it, measure it, and take the file to someone else.

demo.notes: Sofa against the door wall facing the window, so the view is the thing you look at and the door opens behind the seating rather than into it. Armchairs angled at the far corners keep the 0.85 m walkway from door to window clear down the middle. The shelf takes the long solid wall because it is the only wall it fits on at 1.8 m without covering glass. The window wall is the open edge at the far side — it is not modelled, because a wall you cannot move is not part of the layout.

cells.title: Say what this arrangement gives up
cells.intent: Every layout sacrifices something. A plan that does not name its sacrifice is hiding it until you have moved the sofa.
cells.prompt:
This is an arrangement of a room. Say plainly what it optimises for and what it gives up — the thing the household will notice in week three. One or two short paragraphs. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{layout}}
cells.demo:
It optimises for the window. Everything faces it, the walkway runs clear from the door to it, and no tall piece stands between a seat and the light. In a room with one good aspect and no television that is almost certainly the right trade.

What it gives up is conversation. Three seats arranged along a view are three people talking to a window, and the armchairs are far enough apart at the corners that anything said across the room is said loudly. It also puts the shelf on the darkest wall, which is fine for storing books and poor for choosing one. If the room turns out to be used for talking rather than sitting, pull both chairs a metre inward and accept a narrower walkway.

input.label: What you want to build, in the words you would use out loud
input.placeholder: Rough sizes are fine. Say where it goes and what it holds.
input.seed: A shelf for the alcove beside the chimney breast. The alcove is about 900 wide and 380 deep. Four shelves, maybe five. It holds records, so it has to take real weight. Painted, so the timber does not need to be pretty, but no visible fixings.

{{input.thing}}

Shelf spacing 340 mm clear — a 12 inch record is 315 mm, so this clears with a finger's room and no more.
Four shelves, not five: five would put the top shelf above 1.7 m in a 380 mm deep alcove, where records are lifted out blind.

title: Map the Workflow
blurb: Takes how a process gets described out loud and draws it — including the branch nobody mentioned and the loop everyone complains about.
teaches: Diagram — structure drawn out of prose

input.label: How the process gets described, in the words people use
input.placeholder: Write it as someone would say it in a meeting, digressions included.
input.seed: A refund request comes into the shared inbox. Support checks the order, and if it is under £50 they just do it. Over that it goes to a team lead, except at weekends when nobody is on, so it sits. If the item has been used the lead asks for photos, and half the time the customer never sends them, so it sits again. Finance runs the actual refund on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Occasionally support does it themselves anyway because the customer is shouting.

cells.title: Pull the steps out
cells.intent: Spoken process descriptions bury the branches inside asides. This separates them before anything is drawn.
cells.prompt:
Read this description of a process and list each distinct step, decision or wait as its own line, in the order it happens. Include the exceptions and the informal shortcuts — they are part of the process. Do not fix anything. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.process}}

Support checks the order
Decision: is the amount under £50?
Under £50 — support refunds it directly
Over £50 — passed to a team lead
Wait: no team lead at weekends, so it sits
Decision: has the item been used?
Used — lead asks the customer for photos
Wait: photos often never arrive, so it sits again
Approved requests queue for Finance
Finance runs refunds on Tuesdays and Thursdays only
Shortcut: support sometimes refunds over £50 anyway when a customer escalates

cells.title: Draw it
cells.intent: A drawn process is arguable in a way a described one is not. The shortcut everyone uses becomes a line on the page.

demo.note: The escalation shortcut skips the lead entirely.

Auto-reply naming the day it will be looked at

Close it after 7 days with a message saying it can be reopened

Keep the shortcut, log it, review the log monthly

title: Show Me the Shape
blurb: Reads numbers pasted out of a spreadsheet, draws the one chart that answers the question, and states the single claim that chart actually supports.
teaches: Chart — a typed value, not a picture of one

input.label: Paste the numbers, or drop the file they came out of
input.placeholder: Rows, columns, tabs, commas — paste it as it is, and say what you are trying to work out.
input.seed:
Trying to work out whether support cost is actually falling.
Month	Tickets	Cost per ticket
Apr	1820	6.40
May	1910	6.10
Jun	2040	5.80
Jul	2260	5.55
Aug	2510	5.30

cells.title: Read the paste
cells.intent: Pasted data is never clean. Making the parse visible means an error shows up here rather than inside a chart that looks fine.
cells.prompt:
Parse the pasted data into a clean table. Keep every row, name the columns properly, and if a value is ambiguous or missing say so in the cell rather than guessing. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.numbers}}

cells.title: Draw the one chart that answers it
cells.intent: Not every column deserves a chart. Choosing one — and refusing to put two incompatible scales on one axis — is most of the analysis.

demo.note: Both series are indexed to April rather than plotted in their own units — pounds per ticket and pounds per month do not share a scale, and rescaling one to fit the other would invent a crossing point.

cells.title: State the one claim it supports
cells.intent: A chart does not have an opinion. This makes you commit to the sentence you would defend, and to the one you cannot.
cells.demo:
Cost per ticket has fallen every month since April, from £6.40 to £5.30 — 17% off the unit cost in five months, and steady enough month to month that it is unlikely to be noise.

What it does not support is “support is getting cheaper”. On the same index, total spend rose 14%, because volume grew 38% while unit cost fell 17%. Anyone showing the falling line without the rising one is presenting a real efficiency gain and hiding a growing bill. The honest sentence is that efficiency is improving and is not improving fast enough to keep up with volume.

title: Read What Is Printed On It
blurb: Photograph a receipt, label or invoice and get the fields out as a table — with a straight list of what could not be read, rather than a guess.
teaches: Vision for extraction, and the honesty to say what was illegible

input.label: A photo of the thing, and what you need off it
input.placeholder: Attach the picture. Say which fields matter to you.
input.seed: I need the line items and the total for an expense claim. Anything that cannot be read should be flagged, not estimated.
input.seedAlt: Sample till receipt from a timber supplier with one faded line

cells.title: Pull the fields out
cells.intent: Structure straight off the picture. A table you can check line by line against the thing in your hand.
cells.prompt:
Read the attached document and extract its line items as a table. Include quantity, description and amount. Transcribe exactly what is printed; where a character is unreadable, write it as a question mark rather than inferring it. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

What is needed from it: {{input.doc}}

cells.title: Say what could not be read
cells.intent: The failure mode of extraction is a confident wrong number. Naming the illegible parts is the difference between a tool and a liability.
demo: Line 4, DANISH OIL 500ml — the amount is faded; the first digit of the pounds column is unreadable. It is between £10.95 and £19.95.
The operator initials beside the till number are legible as “DANI” but could be a truncated longer name.
The barcode at the foot has not been decoded — reading it from a photograph is not reliable and the invoice number above it says the same thing.
Everything else on the receipt was legible, including the date, invoice number and card last four.

cells.title: Check the arithmetic
cells.intent: The cheapest test of a bad read is whether the numbers add up. It catches the misread digit that nothing else would.
cells.demo:
The legible lines come to 18.40 + 54.00 + 6.16 + 4.25 = £82.81. The stated subtotal is £98.76, leaving £15.95 for the faded line — which fits the visible pattern “1?.95” exactly, so the Danish oil was £15.95. The gap decides the digit; it was not necessary to guess it.

The rest holds: VAT at 20% of £98.76 is £19.752, printed as £19.75, and 98.76 + 19.75 = £118.51, which matches the total. The extraction is arithmetically sound and the one unreadable figure is now determined rather than estimated.

title: Four Ways It Could Look
blurb: Writes four honestly different visual routes out of one brief, draws every one of them, and then makes you say which the brief actually asked for.
teaches: Map over a list — one cell, four pictures, numbered to their inputs

input.label: What the mark is for
input.placeholder: What it stands on, where it will be seen, and what it must not look like.
input.seed: A mark for a small structural engineering practice. Goes on drawings, site boards and a plain website. Must survive being stamped in one colour at 8 mm, and must not look like a tech start-up or a construction franchise.

cells.title: Write four routes that disagree
cells.intent: Four variations of one idea is a formality. These are required to disagree, so what comes back is a choice rather than a mood.
cells.prompt:
Read this brief and write FOUR visual routes that genuinely disagree with each other — different construction, different feeling, each defensible. One dense sentence each, describing subject, geometry, palette and medium concretely enough for a drawing model. No numbering, no preamble. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.mark}}
demo: A hard geometric mark built from a single circle interrupted by one vertical stroke, near-black on warm paper, flat and unshaded — the logic of a section drawing rather than a picture of a building.

A hand-drawn arc repeated three times in warm orange on a near-black ground, the line weight visibly human, with one small solid dot where the arcs meet — engineering as a drawn craft rather than a system.
Flat primary blocks in red, blue and yellow above a single heavy black rule on plain white, with the name set large in a grotesque — Bauhaus plainness, loud at any size.
A fine concentric line engraving in muted green-grey, five rings crossed by four axes with a solid centre, on a cool paper ground — the look of an instrument dial or a surveyor's plate.

cells.title: Draw all four
cells.intent: One cell, four runs, numbered to the routes above. Reading a route and looking at it are different judgements, and only one of them settles anything.
cells.prompt: {{route}}

Hand-drawn route: three repeated orange arcs on near-black with a solid dot
Block route: flat red, blue and yellow squares above a heavy black rule on white
Engraved route: fine concentric rings crossed by four axes in muted green-grey

cells.title: Hold them against the brief
cells.intent: Left alone, people choose the prettiest one. This puts each route back next to the constraint it has to survive.

Close to a dozen existing marks in the sector — the interrupted circle is well used
Yes — one weight, no fills to lose

title: What Was Actually Agreed
blurb: Drop the recording of the meeting. It transcribes on your own machine, then separates what was decided from what was merely said warmly.
teaches: Speech in — a recording becomes text before anything reads it

input.label: The recording, or paste the transcript
input.placeholder: Drop the audio, or paste what was said.
input.seed:
ALEX: So on the pricing change — I think we're aligned that we're not doing it this quarter.
PRIYA: I wouldn't say aligned. I'd say I haven't heard a reason to rush.
ALEX: Fine, not this quarter. Dan, can you get the modelling done before the board thing?
DAN: I can look at it. The board pack is due the fourteenth so realistically it'd be tight.
ALEX: Let's say the fourteenth then.
PRIYA: The other thing is the enterprise tier. We keep saying we'll define it.
ALEX: Yeah. We should really define that.
DAN: Also the churn dashboard is still wrong, the one finance uses.
ALEX: Right. Okay, good meeting everyone.

cells.title: Who committed to what, in their own words
cells.intent: Quote first. Paraphrase is where a hedge quietly becomes a commitment, and the difference is the entire value of reading a transcript.
cells.prompt:
Read this meeting transcript. List every point where a person committed to something, or appeared to, quoting their actual words. Attribute each one. Do not clean up hedges — if someone said “I can look at it”, that is what they said. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{input.meeting}}
demo: ALEX: “we're not doing it this quarter” — stated as a shared position before anyone agreed to it.
PRIYA: “I wouldn't say aligned. I'd say I haven't heard a reason to rush.” — an explicit refusal of the word aligned.
DAN: “I can look at it.” — offered when asked to get modelling done. Not the same verb.
DAN: “the board pack is due the fourteenth so realistically it'd be tight.” — a warning, immediately converted by someone else into a date.
ALEX: “Let's say the fourteenth then.” — a deadline set by the person not doing the work.
ALEX: “We should really define that.” — no owner, no date, no verb belonging to anybody.

cells.title: Decisions, owners, and how solid each one is
cells.intent: The table people think they are getting from notes. The last column is the one that matters — most rows in most meetings are not actually agreed.
cells.prompt:
From these quotes, build the decision table: what was decided, who owns it, by when, and how solid it actually is — Agreed, Assumed, or Not agreed — with one line saying why you graded it that way. Respond in {{locale.outputLanguage}}.

{{said}}

rows: Agreed — nobody objected, and Priya's objection was to the word, not the decision
Assumed — Dan said he could look at it and warned it was tight; the date was set by Alex, not accepted by Dan
Not agreed — “we should really define that” has no owner and no date, and this is at least the second meeting it has survived
Not agreed — raised by Dan, acknowledged with “Right”, and never picked up

cells.title: What was raised and left open
cells.intent: The things that get dropped are rarely the unimportant ones — they are the ones nobody wanted to own in the room.
demo: The enterprise tier definition — closed by one name against it before the meeting ends, or by an explicit decision that it waits until Q3.
The churn dashboard finance relies on — closed by finding out whether anyone owns that dashboard at all, which is the real question underneath.
Whether Dan actually accepted the 14th — closed by asking him, in writing, today.
Whether “not this quarter” means the decision is revisited next quarter or is settled — nobody said, and the two readings lead to different work.
